title: Linked list cycle
prompt: Does a linked list loop back on itself? Try to use O(1) memory.
explanation: Move one pointer one step at a time and another two steps. If there's a cycle, the fast one laps the slow one and they meet. If not, fast reaches the end.
steps: slow = fast = head.
While fast && fast.next: move slow 1, fast 2.
If they're ever the same node, there's a cycle.
hint: Two runners on a circular track, one twice as fast. What eventually happens?

title: Binary tree level order traversal
prompt: Return a tree's values level by level, top to bottom.
explanation: BFS with a queue visits nodes level by level. Record the queue's length at the start of each level so you know where the level ends.
steps: Start the queue with the root.
Read size = queue.length, then pop exactly size nodes into this level's list.
Push each popped node's children, then repeat for the next level.
gotcha: In JavaScript, shift() is O(n). For big inputs, use an index pointer into the array instead.
hint: Which traversal naturally visits nodes in order of their distance from the root?

title: Number of islands
prompt: A grid of land and water. Count the islands, where land connects up, down, left and right.
explanation: Every unvisited land cell starts a new island. Flood-fill from it to mark the whole island, so you never count it again.
steps: Scan every cell.
On unvisited land, increase the count and DFS/BFS through its four neighbors.
Mark cells as visited (or set them to water) as you go.

complexity.space: O(m·n) worst case for the stack or queue

gotcha: Recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a huge all-land grid. An explicit stack avoids that.
hint: An island is a connected group of cells. How do you visit a whole group exactly once?

title: Number of provinces
prompt: Given which cities are directly connected, count the groups of cities that are connected directly or indirectly.
explanation: This is counting connected components. Union-Find merges each connected pair and counts the remaining roots. DFS from each unvisited city works too.
steps: Give every city its own parent.
For each connected pair, union(a, b), and decrease the count when the roots differ.
The remaining count is the answer.
gotcha: Without path compression in find, Union-Find can degrade to O(n) per call.
hint: Groups of things joined by "is connected to". Which structure merges groups cheaply?

title: Course schedule
prompt: Courses have prerequisites. Can you finish all of them?
explanation: Prerequisites form a directed graph. You can finish everything if and only if the graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm finds out by repeatedly taking courses with no remaining prerequisites.
steps: Build an adjacency list and an in-degree count for each course.
Queue every course with in-degree 0. Pop one and decrement its neighbors, queueing any that reach 0.
If you processed every course, there's no cycle.
hint: Prerequisites form a directed graph. You can finish everything only if the graph has no ...?

title: Implement a trie
prompt: Build a structure with insert, search for a whole word, and startsWith for a prefix.
explanation: Each node maps a character to a child node and has an end flag. Words with a common prefix share a path.
steps: Node = { children: Map, end: false }.
Insert: walk or create children for each char, then set end = true.
Search walks the path and checks end. startsWith just checks that the path exists.
gotcha: search('app') must be false if only 'apple' was inserted. That's what the end flag is for.
hint: Words that share a prefix should share storage for that prefix.

title: Permutations
prompt: Return every ordering of a list of distinct numbers.
explanation: Build one ordering at a time: choose an unused number, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts clean.
steps: Recurse with the current path and a used set.
When the path is full, push a copy of it.
Otherwise, for each unused number: add it, recurse, remove it.
gotcha: Push [...path], not path, or every result ends up as the same emptied array.

title: Coin change
prompt: Fewest coins needed to make an amount, with unlimited coins of each value. Return -1 if it can't be done.
explanation: The best answer for amount a is 1 + the best for a - coin, over every coin. Greedy (largest coin first) fails, for example coins [1, 3, 4] for amount 6.
steps: dp[0] = 0, and every other entry = Infinity.
For a from 1 to amount, for each coin ≤ a: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1).
Return dp[amount], or -1 if it's still Infinity.
gotcha: Greedy looks right and passes simple examples. Have a counterexample ready.
hint: If you knew the best answer for every smaller amount, how would you get this one?

title: Longest common subsequence
prompt: Length of the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order (not necessarily contiguous).
explanation: 2D DP over prefixes. If the last characters match, extend the diagonal. If not, take the better of dropping one character from either string.
steps: dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i chars of a and the first j chars of b.
If a[i-1] === b[j-1]: dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
The answer is dp[m][n].

complexity.space: O(m·n), or O(n) with one row

hint: Compare the last characters of each prefix. What happens when they match, and when they don't?

title: Jump game
prompt: Each number is the furthest you can jump from that spot. Can you reach the last index?
explanation: Track the furthest index you can reach so far. If you ever stand on an index past that, you're stuck. DP works too but is O(n²).
steps: reach = 0.
For each i: if i > reach, return false. Otherwise reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).
Return true after the loop.
hint: You don't need the exact route. One running number tells you everything.
